label: Roles blur into builders
title: Product and design now commit code too
thesis: Product managers and designers are starting to produce working software with agents, which blurs the line between who specifies software and who builds it. Engineers' work moves towards providing the architecture, building blocks and review that let others do this safely.
construct: Who in a software organisation produces working software - the share of product, design and other non-engineering roles that ship running prototypes or commits - and what engineers do in response. Not total AI tool adoption by non-engineers, headcount of any role, or hiring of new roles, which move without anyone outside engineering shipping code.
currentPressure: Agents make implementation cheap enough for non-engineers to attempt, while the cost of deciding what to build and keeping architecture coherent has not fallen.

implications.statement: Engineers shift toward supplying the primitives, architecture and APIs others build on and reviewing what agents and non-engineers produce inside them, becoming 'custodians rather than contributors'.
When product managers build working prototypes themselves (20-25 PMs, about one per fifteen engineers, at Redis) the specification arrives as a running artefact and changes what an engineer receives.
Changes by non-engineers can each look defensible and still damage the architecture together, so someone has to own system-level coherence explicitly.

evidence.note: InfoQ panel of named practitioners: one reports product and design colleagues committing code 'just as freely as engineers'; engineers building platforms for agents and review; panel reports from their own organisations
Redis: ~20-25 product managers (about one per fifteen engineers) build working React and Claude Code prototypes themselves; specification moves from a document to a running artefact

DHH on the Basecamp experiment: designers used agents to implement changes directly; the PRs looked individually defensible but collectively damaged architecture and developers restored coherence by hand. Attached for designers shipping, and the architectural cost is the caution

Linear, 166,000 paid users: share attaching a PR in 30 days rose 3% to 10% for product managers and 1% to 8% for designers, mostly June 2025-June 2026; 'attaching' is undefined and may include linking others' PRs

reachRationale: Seen in three forerunner organisations (an InfoQ panel's employers, Redis, 37signals' Basecamp experiment), one of which found the output harmful to architecture. No source shows this as common practice. Linear's data on 166,000 users gives the first count: the share of product managers and designers attaching pull requests roughly tripled in a year, to 10% and 8%. The measure is loose, since attaching may mean linking a change someone else wrote.
whatWouldChangeThis: Counts of commits or merged changes by non-engineer roles showing they stay a small, flat share
Evidence that non-engineer changes are routinely reverted or rewritten by engineers
Organisations that tried this and re-established a hard boundary between specification and implementation
